Made easy

Built to be simple, friendly, and fun

No clutter, no head-scratching. Open the app, find a trail, and go — everything works the way you'd expect, in plain words.

A map that walks with you

On a hike, a little nutmeg marks where you stand — and it turns as you turn, so you always know which way you're facing. A compass rides on the side of the map, so north and south are never a guess.

Trail lines you can trust

Trail lines are drawn from official Connecticut sources. And when a trail has no line yet, hikers can share the path from their own recordings — so the map keeps getting better, one hike at a time.

Rate trails in nutmegs, not stars

Finished a hike? Tap the nutmegs to rate it — one to five — because this is Connecticut, after all.

Save trails with the nutmeg button

Spot a trail you want to try later? One tap on the nutmeg button saves it to your list, ready when you are.

The name

Why “Nutmeg”?

Connecticut is called the Nutmeg State for its early Yankee peddlers, who sold nutmegs traded through its ports. Legend has it some carved wooden nutmegs that passed for the real spice — and the name stuck as a badge of Connecticut ingenuity.

Connecticut & nutmeg history

A small state with a long memory

The trails in this app cross land that Connecticut people have been walking, working, and telling stories about for centuries.

The nutmeg story

In Connecticut's early days, nutmeg was a prized spice that arrived by ship through the state's ports. Yankee peddlers carried those nutmegs from town to town, selling them door to door — and built a reputation for sharp, inventive trading.

Legend has it that some peddlers carved wooden nutmegs so convincing they passed for the real spice. Whether every tale is true or not, the name stuck — not as an insult, but as a badge of Connecticut ingenuity.

Connecticut carries two nicknames today: the “Nutmeg State,” the beloved traditional one, and the official “Constitution State.” We picked the one that smells like the woods.

Trails with deep roots

Connecticut built one of America's oldest state park systems — its first park land was acquired at Sherwood Island in 1914, and the parks have been growing ever since.

The famous blue blazes came a little later. The Blue-Blazed Hiking Trail System has been maintained by the Connecticut Forest & Park Association since 1929 — generations of volunteers painting blazes, clearing blowdowns, and keeping hundreds of miles of trail open for everyone.

When you follow a blue blaze, you're walking a line of care that stretches back nearly a hundred years.

Featured trails

Trails with stories

Twelve favorites from the app — fugitive judges, a devil's footprints, Connecticut's last wolf, dinosaur tracks, two mountaintop towers, a canal, and a ghost train. Each one is worth the walk for the story alone.

Sleeping Giant State Park · Hamden

Tower Trail

The long traprock ridge north of New Haven really does look like a giant lying down for a nap — head, chest, belly, and legs stretched across the skyline.

The story: In Quinnipiac legend, the ridge is Hobbomock, a giant turned to stone. The stone tower on his chest was built in 1936–1939, and the view from the top is still the reward.

See the Tower Trail in the app →

Gillette Castle State Park · East Haddam

The Castle Grounds

Easy walking paths circle a stone “castle” above the Connecticut River — part home, part stage set, all character.

The story: Actor William Gillette, famous for playing Sherlock Holmes on stage, built this castle-like home in 1914–1919. It became a state park in 1943.

See Gillette Castle's trails in the app →

Kent Falls State Park · Kent

The Falls Trail

A short climb alongside one of Connecticut's prettiest waterfalls, with viewing spots at every level of the cascade.

The story: The brook drops about 250 feet in a staircase of cascades — and falls like these once powered local mills, turning falling water into work.

See the Kent Falls Steps Trail in the app →

Appalachian Trail · Salisbury

Bear Mountain

Connecticut's stretch of the Appalachian Trail crosses the state's wild northwest corner — and tops out on its highest summit.

The story: About 51 miles of the A.T. run through Connecticut, climbing Bear Mountain (2,316 ft), the highest summit in the state. The full Appalachian Trail was completed in 1937.

See the Bear Mountain hike in the app →

West Rock Ridge State Park · New Haven / Hamden

Regicides Trail & Judges Cave

A blue-blazed trail runs the length of the West Rock ridge — and partway along it, a jumble of giant boulders forms a small rock shelter with an outsized place in history.

The story: In 1661, Edward Whalley and William Goffe — two of the judges who had signed King Charles I's death warrant — hid in this cave from agents of Charles II, sent to arrest them. The roughly 7-mile trail along the ridge is still named for them: the Regicides Trail.

See the Regicides Trail in the app →

Devil's Hopyard State Park · East Haddam

Chapman Falls

The Eightmile River pours over a 60-foot staircase of rock in the middle of the woods — and the round holes worn into the stone below the falls come with a devilish explanation.

The story: Early settlers said the smooth, round potholes were the Devil's hoofprints, left when he sat on the rocks, got his tail wet in the cold water, and stomped off in a rage. The falls also did honest work, powering Beebe's Mills into the 1890s — and the state bought the land in 1919 to make the park.

See Devil's Hopyard's trails in the app →

Mashamoquet Brook State Park · Pomfret

The Wolf Den

Tucked between boulders on the brook trail is a low, dark crack in the rock — the den at the center of Connecticut's most famous frontier tale. Even the park's name is a story: Mashamoquet is Mohegan for “stream of good fishing.”

The story: In 1742, a wolf had been raiding local farms, and Israel Putnam — later a major general in the Revolutionary War — tracked it here, crept into the den by torchlight, and shot the animal legend calls Connecticut's last wolf. The Wolf Den is now on the National Register of Historic Places.

See the Mashamoquet Brook Trail in the app →

Dinosaur State Park · Rocky Hill

The Dinosaur Tracks

Under a dome in Rocky Hill lies a sandstone floor covered in three-toed footprints — a walkway laid down by dinosaurs some 200 million years ago, found entirely by accident.

The story: On August 23, 1966, bulldozer operator Edward McCarthy was excavating for a new state building when he uncovered the tracks — about 2,000 Eubrontes footprints in all. The state founded the park just weeks later, and in 1968 it became a National Natural Landmark.

See Dinosaur State Park's trails in the app →

Hubbard Park · Meriden

Castle Craig

A 32-foot stone tower crowns East Peak, high above Meriden — climb it on a clear day and the view runs from Long Island Sound to the hills of Massachusetts.

The story: The tower was dedicated on October 29, 1900, a gift to the people of Meriden from industrialist Walter Hubbard, whose generosity created the whole 1,800-acre park — designed with help from the famous Olmsted firm. It remains one of the most-loved landmarks on the Metacomet Ridge.

See the Castle Craig hike in the app →

Talcott Mountain State Park · Simsbury

Heublein Tower

A 165-foot white tower rises from the Talcott Mountain ridge — part summer home, part castle, and still the best seat in the Farmington Valley.

The story: Gilbert Heublein built the tower in 1914 as his summer home, keeping a promise made while hiking here to build his wife “a castle on the mountain.” It was engineered to withstand 100 mph winds and held Connecticut's first home elevator. The state bought it in 1966 and opened the park in 1974.

See the Tower Trail in the app →

Farmington Canal State Park Trail · Cheshire / Hamden

Lock 12 & the Farmington Canal

Today it's a shady, paved greenway — but the path beside restored Lock 12 in Cheshire was once a water highway, where boats climbed the valley one lock at a time.

The story: Construction on the Farmington Canal began on July 4, 1825; the first boats floated in 1828, and by 1835 the canal reached Northampton, Massachusetts, through 28 locks in Connecticut alone. Railroads later took over the route — and today it lives on as the Farmington Canal Heritage Trail.

See the Farmington Canal Trail in the app →

Air Line State Park Trail · East Hampton

The Air Line & the Ghost Train

The trail crosses the Lyman Viaduct high above the valley floor — an earthen bridge built for a railroad that promised the straightest line between New York and Boston.

The story: Built in the late 1860s and finished in 1873, the Air Line took its name from that straight-as-an-arrow “air line” route. From 1891, its crack express — the New England Limited, all white-and-gold Pullman cars — swept through the night so ghostly that people called it the Ghost Train. Passenger service ended in 1902; the rails are gone, but the viaducts and the trail remain.

See the Air Line Trail in the app →

  • Optional hometown
  • Optional profile photo
  • Selected avatar color
  • Account preferences
  • Subscription status

We use this information to create and maintain your account, personalize your experience, and provide access to app features.

B. Location and GPS Information

With your permission, Nutmeg Trails accesses your device’s location to provide hiking-related features.

Location information may include:

  • Current GPS coordinates
  • Hiking routes and recorded paths
  • Starting and ending locations
  • Distance traveled
  • Hike duration
  • Location points associated with recorded hikes

This information helps you navigate trails, record hiking activity, and review previous hikes.

Your device’s operating system controls location permissions.

C. Hiking Activity

When you record a hike or interact with hiking features, we may collect:

  • Recorded hiking routes
  • Hike dates and times
  • Distance traveled
  • Duration of hikes
  • Trail ratings
  • Hiking history
  • Photos voluntarily uploaded
  • Trail contributions you choose to share

This information supports your personal hiking records and community features.

D. Photos and User-Generated Content

You may choose to upload photos or contribute content to Nutmeg Trails.

Depending on the feature, this may include:

  • Hiking photographs
  • Profile pictures
  • Trail ratings
  • Shared hiking routes

Content you intentionally publish through public features may be visible to other Nutmeg Trails users.

Please avoid uploading photographs or information that reveal sensitive personal details.

E. Subscription Information

Nutmeg Trails may offer premium features through its Summit subscription.

When you purchase a subscription through Apple:

  • Apple processes your payment.
  • Nutmeg Trails receives information necessary to verify your subscription status and provide access to premium features.
  • We do not receive or store your full credit card number or payment card security code.

Apple’s own privacy practices apply to information collected and processed through its payment services.

3. HOW WE USE YOUR INFORMATION

We use collected information to:

  1. Create, authenticate, and manage user accounts.
  2. Provide hiking maps and navigation features.
  3. Record and display hiking routes.
  4. Maintain personal hiking histories.
  5. Display photos and trail ratings submitted by users.
  6. Enable voluntary sharing of hiking routes.
  7. Verify subscriptions and provide premium features.
  8. Send essential account and service communications.
  9. Respond to support requests.
  10. Maintain the reliability, functionality, and security of the Services.
  11. Investigate misuse and enforce applicable policies.
  12. Comply with applicable legal obligations.

We do not sell your personal information.

We do not use your personal hiking routes for targeted advertising.

4. LOCATION PRIVACY AND GPS TRACKING

Location information is an important part of the Nutmeg Trails experience.

We recognize that precise location information can be sensitive.

A. Location Permission

Nutmeg Trails requests your permission before accessing your device’s location.

You can manage location permissions through your device’s settings.

B. Active Hiking Sessions

When you start recording a hike, Nutmeg Trails uses location information to document your route, distance, and hiking activity.

If background location access is enabled and supported, location recording may continue during an active hike when your device is locked or another application is open.

C. When You Are Not Recording a Hike

Nutmeg Trails does not continuously record your hiking movements when no hiking recording session is active.

Location access for other map-related features, if applicable, depends on the permissions you provide and the feature you are using.

D. Saved Hiking Routes

Recorded hiking routes may be associated with your account so you can access your hiking history.

E. Public Route Sharing

Your recorded hiking routes are not automatically published as public trails.

A recorded route becomes publicly available only when you deliberately choose to share it through the app’s sharing features.

Please remember that sharing a GPS route may reveal sensitive locations, including your starting point, ending point, or places you frequently visit.

F. Disabling Location Access

You may disable or modify location permissions at any time through your device settings.

Disabling location access may limit certain features, including live navigation and hike recording.

5. HOW WE SHARE INFORMATION

Nutmeg Trails respects your privacy.

We do not sell, rent, or trade personal information to advertisers or data brokers.

We may share information in the following circumstances:

A. Information You Choose to Share

When you voluntarily publish a hiking route, photo, or trail rating, that information may become visible to other users.

You are responsible for reviewing information before making it public.

B. Service Providers

We work with trusted technology providers that help operate Nutmeg Trails.

These include:

Supabase

Provides account authentication, database services, and data storage.

Brevo

Provides email delivery services for account-related communications, including welcome messages and password assistance.

Apple

Processes subscriptions and manages applicable in-app purchases.

These providers process information as necessary to deliver their respective services.

We expect service providers handling personal information on our behalf to maintain appropriate privacy and security protections.

C. Legal Requirements

We may disclose information when reasonably necessary to:

  • Comply with applicable laws.
  • Respond to valid legal requests.
  • Protect the rights and security of Nutmeg Trails.
  • Investigate suspected fraud or misuse.
  • Protect users or others from serious harm.

6. DATA SECURITY

We take reasonable administrative, technical, and organizational measures designed to protect personal information against unauthorized access, disclosure, alteration, and loss.

Our security practices include the use of established technology providers for account management and data storage.

However, no internet-based service or electronic storage system can guarantee absolute security.

We encourage users to protect their account credentials and notify us if they suspect unauthorized account activity.

For security concerns, contact:

support@nutmegtrails.com

7. DATA RETENTION

We retain personal information for as long as reasonably necessary to provide the Services, maintain your account, fulfill the purposes described in this policy, and comply with applicable legal obligations.

Information associated with your hiking history may remain in your account until you delete the relevant information or request account deletion.

When information is no longer required, we take reasonable steps to delete or de-identify it, subject to applicable legal requirements and technical limitations.

Certain information may be retained for a limited period when reasonably necessary for security, fraud prevention, dispute resolution, or legal compliance.

8. YOUR PRIVACY RIGHTS AND CHOICES

You have choices regarding your personal information.

Depending on applicable law and the features available in your account, you may request to:

  • Access personal information associated with your account.
  • Correct inaccurate account information.
  • Delete your account.
  • Request deletion of personal information.
  • Withdraw permission for location access.
  • Manage information you choose to share publicly.
  • Ask questions about how your information is processed.

To submit a privacy request, contact:

support@nutmegtrails.com

We may request reasonable verification of your identity before processing requests involving account information.

We will respond in accordance with applicable law.

9. ACCOUNT DELETION

You may request deletion of your Nutmeg Trails account and associated personal information.

To request deletion, contact:

support@nutmegtrails.com

Account deletion generally includes removal of personal information associated with your account, subject to applicable legal obligations and limited retention requirements.

If account deletion is available directly within the app, you may also initiate the process through the applicable account settings.

Information you previously shared publicly may be subject to additional removal processes, including deletion of associated photos, ratings, and route contributions, as required by applicable policies and law.

Please note that deleting your Nutmeg Trails account does not automatically cancel an active subscription managed by Apple.

Apple subscriptions must be managed separately through your Apple account settings.

10. CHILDREN’S PRIVACY

Nutmeg Trails is not intended for children under the age of 13.

We do not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13.

If we become aware that we have collected personal information from a child under 13 without appropriate authorization, we will take reasonable steps to delete that information.

Parents or guardians who believe a child has provided personal information may contact:

support@nutmegtrails.com

11. THIRD-PARTY SERVICES AND LINKS

Nutmeg Trails may contain links to external websites, mapping resources, or other third-party services.

These services operate independently and may maintain their own privacy policies.

We encourage users to review the privacy practices of third-party services before providing personal information.

Nutmeg Trails is not responsible for the privacy practices of independent third-party websites or applications.

12. WEBSITE TECHNOLOGIES

Our website may use technologies necessary to operate its features, maintain user sessions, and support account access.

Depending on the technologies implemented, these may include cookies or similar browser-based storage.

Where applicable, information about optional analytics or other nonessential technologies will be provided through appropriate notices or privacy controls.

We do not use personal information collected through Nutmeg Trails for targeted advertising.

13. INTERNATIONAL USERS

Nutmeg Trails primarily serves hikers exploring Connecticut and other supported locations.

If you access our Services from outside the United States, your information may be processed or stored in the United States or other locations where our service providers operate.

Privacy and data protection laws may differ between countries.

Where applicable, we will process personal information in accordance with relevant data protection requirements.

14. CHANGES TO THIS PRIVACY POLICY

We may update this Privacy Policy to reflect:

  • Changes to app features.
  • New technologies or service providers.
  • Changes in legal requirements.
  • Updates to our information practices.

When changes occur, we will update the “Last Updated” date at the beginning of this policy.

If changes materially affect how we handle personal information, we will provide additional notice when required by applicable law.

We encourage users to review this policy periodically.

15. CONTACT US

If you have questions, concerns, or requests regarding this Privacy Policy or your personal information, please contact:

Nutmeg Trails
Operated by Reginald Campbell Jr.
Connecticut, United States

Email: support@nutmegtrails.com

Website: https://nutmegtrails.com

We appreciate your trust in Nutmeg Trails and are committed to providing an enjoyable outdoor experience while respecting your privacy.

Explore Connecticut. Discover New Trails. Protect Your Privacy.
